name: Tesa/IPA Protocol

lead: Tesa/IPA stacks two growth-hormone-axis peptides, tesamorelin and ipamorelin, and is used for fat loss, especially around the midsection, and a leaner look.

Tesamorelin mimics growth-hormone-releasing hormone and ipamorelin acts on the ghrelin receptor, so both raise growth hormone and IGF-1 through different routes. Tesamorelin is a prescription drug approved for HIV-associated lipodystrophy, where trials looked at visceral fat. Ipamorelin was developed for postoperative ileus and dropped. No trial has tested the combination.

paras: In peptide circles the stack is run alongside diet and training for body composition, with fat-loss changes described over weeks to months. Tesamorelin is prescription-only and ipamorelin is typically sold as a research peptide.

Tesamorelin effects reported in its use include injection-site reactions, edema, joint pain and glucose intolerance. Ipamorelin is unapproved and on the WADA prohibited list. The combination has no safety data.

angle.text: Tesa/IPA aims at a leaner midsection: both peptides raise growth hormone, which is linked to less visceral fat. Tesamorelin has trial data for visceral fat in a specific patient group; the combination has not been trialled.

lead: The Tesa/IPA protocol is a term used in peptide and body-composition circles for combining two injectable growth-hormone-axis peptides, tesamorelin and ipamorelin. The two are different substances: tesamorelin is a synthetic analogue of growth-hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH), while ipamorelin is a pentapeptide that acts on the ghrelin (growth hormone secretagogue) receptor. [1][2]

Tesamorelin is a prescription drug sold by Theratechnologies as Egrifta, initially approved in 2010 for HIV-associated lipodystrophy. [1] Ipamorelin was developed by Novo Nordisk, later tested by Helsinn Therapeutics for postoperative ileus, and abandoned for lack of efficacy; it is not an approved drug and is commonly sold as a research peptide. [2]

Proponents pair the two on the theory that they release growth hormone through different receptors and could be used for fat loss. No published trial has tested the combination in humans, and the sources reviewed describe neither agent as an approved cosmetic treatment. [1][2]
infobox: Combination of two peptides (GHRH analogue plus ghrelin-receptor agonist)
US prescription drug, approved 2010 for HIV lipodystrophy [1]
Unapproved; sold as a research peptide [2]

paras: Tesamorelin consists of the full 44 amino acids of human GHRH with a trans-3-hexenoic acid group added, which makes it more potent and more resistant to breakdown than natural GHRH. It stimulates the body's own growth hormone release, raising IGF-1, and its main effect on body fat is lipolysis. [1]

Reported adverse effects include injection-site redness and itching, peripheral edema, diarrhea and joint or limb pain; it may cause glucose intolerance and raise type 2 diabetes risk, and it is contraindicated in pregnancy and in patients with hypothalamic-pituitary disruption. [1]

Ipamorelin is a synthetic pentapeptide derived from GHRP-1 that selectively agonises the ghrelin receptor. It raises plasma growth hormone in animals and humans and, unlike GHRP-2 and GHRP-6, is reported not to stimulate ACTH or cortisol. Its elimination half-life is about two hours. [2]
Helsinn's phase II program for postoperative ileus stopped because of lack of efficacy. It appears among WADA-prohibited substances and has been used by athletes as a performance-enhancing drug. [2]

The pairing is discussed as a way to lower body fat without a standard weight-loss drug, on the reasoning that a GHRH analogue and a secretagogue stimulate growth hormone release by complementary routes. The sources reviewed do not document any controlled evaluation of that reasoning.

No studies found. Tesamorelin has been studied for HIV-associated lipodystrophy, and ipamorelin in a postoperative ileus trial and a healthy-volunteer pharmacokinetic study, but not together and not for cosmetic purposes. [1][2]
